```{r}
#| include: false
has_ggplot <- rlang::is_installed("ggplot2")
```


tidymst reads the Excel files that NanoTemper's MO.Affinity Analysis
software exports from microscale thermophoresis (MST) experiments, and turns
them into ordinary R data frames. From there you can recalculate Fnorm, fit
binding curves to get a Kd, and make your own plots.

This guide walks through a whole analysis. It assumes you have used R a
little, for example to make a basic plot, but not much more.

## Setup

Install tidymst from GitHub (you only need to do this once):

```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("BradyAJohnston/tidymst")
```

Then load it at the start of every script, along with dplyr (for working with
data frames) and ggplot2 (for plotting):

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
library(tidymst)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Exporting your data from MO.Affinity Analysis

tidymst reads the `.xlsx` files that MO.Affinity Analysis writes when you
export data. Which export you need depends on what you want to do:

| To get                                   | Export from                          | Read with                    |
|------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------|------------------------------|
| The MST trace of every capillary         | MST Traces                           | `read_mst_traces()`          |
| The Fnorm of every capillary             | Dose-Response (Flat)                 | `read_mst_dose_response()`   |
| Mean responses, and MO.Affinity's fit    | Compare Results (Chart)              | `read_mst_dose_response()`, `read_mst_fit()` |
| A table of MO.Affinity's fits            | Compare Results (Grid)               | `read_mst_fit()`             |
| The capillary scans                      | Capillary Scan                       | `read_mst_capillary_scan()`  |

If you're not sure what a file is, `read_mst()` works it out for you and
picks the right reader.

The MST Traces export is the most useful: it has the raw data and records
which capillaries you marked as outliers, so you can redo the whole analysis
in R.

## Reading data

tidymst comes with some example files, from an experiment measuring the
binding of a protein (dPPR10-Cy5) to two RNAs (atpH-fl and NEAT1-fl).
`tidymst_example()` gives the path to one of them:

```{r}
path <- tidymst_example("dppr10-cy5_traces.xlsx")
```

With your own data, `path` is just the location of your file, in quotes:

```{r}
#| eval: false
path <- "C:/Users/me/Documents/MST/2024-05-01_traces.xlsx"
```

Read the traces with `read_mst_traces()`:

```{r}
traces <- read_mst_traces(path)
traces
```

The result is a *tibble*, a kind of data frame. Each row is one time point
from one capillary, and each column is one variable. The columns are the same
whichever file you read:

* `merge_set`, `run` and `capillary` say where the measurement came from.
* `target`, `target_concentration`, `ligand` and `ligand_concentration`
  describe the sample. Concentrations are always in molar (M), so 50 nM is
  `5e-08`.
* `included` is `FALSE` for capillaries you marked as outliers.
* `time` (in seconds) and `fluorescence` are the trace itself.

To see the whole table in RStudio or Positron, use `View(traces)`. To pull out
one column, use `$`:

```{r}
unique(traces$target)
```

## Looking at the traces

`mst_plot_traces()` draws every trace, coloured by ligand concentration:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_ggplot
mst_plot_traces(traces)
```

The traces for the two RNAs are drawn on top of each other. To split them
into separate panels, add `facet_wrap()` with `+`, as with any ggplot:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_ggplot
mst_plot_traces(traces) +
  facet_wrap(~target)
```

## Calculating Fnorm

Fnorm compares the fluorescence after the IR laser switches on (the "hot"
window) to before it (the "cold" window). It's given in per mille (‰), so 1000
means no change.

MO.Affinity Analysis records the windows it used, which you can see with
`read_mst_metadata()`:

```{r}
read_mst_metadata(path) |>
  select(cold_start, cold_end, hot_start, hot_end)
```

The `|>` symbol is called the *pipe*. It passes the result on the left into
the function on the right, so you can read the code as "read the metadata,
*then* select these columns".

`mst_fnorm()` calculates Fnorm for each capillary. First, use `filter()` to
keep only the capillaries that weren't marked as outliers:

```{r}
fnorm <- traces |>
  filter(included) |>
  mst_fnorm(hot = c(19, 20), cold = c(-1, 0))

fnorm
```

Now there is one row per capillary, and the Fnorm is in the `response`
column. These values match those MO.Affinity Analysis calculates for the same
windows, but here you are free to try others, such as `hot = c(1.5, 2.5)`.

## Fitting a binding curve

`mst_fit()` fits a binding model to the Fnorm values. Use `.by` to fit each
RNA separately:

```{r}
fits <- mst_fit(fnorm, model = "kd", .by = target)
fits
```

There's one row per RNA. `n` is the number of capillaries fitted and
`sigma` is the scatter of the points around the curve. The warning tells us
that one fit failed: NEAT1-fl's `fit` is empty (`NULL`). As we'll see in the
plot below, NEAT1-fl's Fnorm barely changes with concentration, so there is no
binding curve to fit. A failed fit is never an error, so one bad group won't
stop the others being fitted.

There are two models:

* `model = "kd"` (the default) fits the standard 1:1 binding model, taking
  into account the concentration of the fluorescent target.
* `model = "hill"` fits the Hill equation, giving an EC50 and Hill
  coefficient, for cooperative binding.

By default, the Kd model estimates the target concentration too. If you know
it, setting it gives a more reliable Kd, for example
`mst_fit(fnorm, target_concentration = 50e-9, .by = target)`.

The `fit` column holds the fitted models. Get the fitted values with
`mst_coefs()`:

```{r}
coefs <- mst_coefs(fits)
coefs
```

Each row is one parameter (`term`) of one fit, with its `estimate`, standard
error and 95% confidence interval. To get just the Kds, in nM:

```{r}
coefs |>
  filter(term == "kd") |>
  mutate(kd_nM = estimate * 1e9) |>
  select(target, kd_nM)
```

atpH-fl binds with a Kd of around 13 nM, matching the value MO.Affinity
Analysis gives for the same data. Always plot your data to check a fit!

## Plotting dose-response curves

`mst_plot_dose_response()` plots the data, with the fitted curves if you give
it `fits`:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_ggplot
mst_plot_dose_response(fnorm, fits, colour = target)
```

## Comparing curves with fraction bound

Different targets often have different baselines, which makes them hard to
compare. `mst_normalise()` adds two columns using the fits:

* `delta_fnorm`: Fnorm relative to the unbound state, so every curve starts
  at 0.
* `fraction_bound`: the fraction of target bound, from 0 (unbound) to 1
  (fully bound).

```{r}
normalised <- mst_normalise(fnorm, fits)
normalised |>
  select(target, ligand_concentration, response, delta_fnorm, fraction_bound)
```

NEAT1-fl has no fit, so its `delta_fnorm` and `fraction_bound` are `NA`
(missing).

## Making your own plots

The plotting functions in tidymst are a quick way to look at your data, but
for a figure you'll probably want to make your own. Because every function
returns an ordinary data frame, you can plot them with ggplot2 like any other
data.

A ggplot is built in layers, added with `+`:

1. `ggplot()` says which data to use, and `aes()` which columns go on which
   axis or colour.
2. `geom_*()` functions draw things: `geom_point()` for points,
   `geom_line()` for lines.
3. Other functions change the scales, labels and appearance.

Here is a plot of the fraction bound for atpH-fl, step by step. First, keep
just the atpH-fl data, and convert the concentration to nM, which reads better
on an axis:

```{r}
atph <- normalised |>
  filter(target == "atpH-fl") |>
  mutate(concentration_nM = ligand_concentration * 1e9)
```

Then plot the points, with the concentration on a log scale:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_ggplot
ggplot(atph, aes(x = concentration_nM, y = fraction_bound)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10()
```

To add the fitted curve, get its points with `mst_curve()`. It has the same
columns as the data (`ligand_concentration`, `response`, `delta_fnorm`,
`fraction_bound`), so convert it the same way:

```{r}
curve <- mst_curve(fits) |>
  filter(target == "atpH-fl") |>
  mutate(concentration_nM = ligand_concentration * 1e9)
```

Now add it as a line. Each layer can use its own data, given with `data =`:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_ggplot
ggplot(atph, aes(x = concentration_nM, y = fraction_bound)) +
  geom_line(data = curve) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(
    x = "dPPR10-Cy5 concentration (nM)",
    y = "Fraction bound",
    title = "dPPR10-Cy5 binding to atpH-fl"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

The individual capillaries can look noisy. To plot the mean and standard
deviation of each concentration instead, summarise the data first. `.by`
makes `summarise()` calculate the mean and standard deviation separately for
each concentration:

```{r}
atph_mean <- atph |>
  summarise(
    mean = mean(fraction_bound),
    sd = sd(fraction_bound),
    .by = concentration_nM
  )
atph_mean
```

Then draw error bars with `geom_errorbar()`:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_ggplot
ggplot(atph_mean, aes(x = concentration_nM, y = mean)) +
  geom_line(data = curve, aes(y = fraction_bound)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - sd, ymax = mean + sd), width = 0.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "dPPR10-Cy5 concentration (nM)", y = "Fraction bound") +
  theme_bw()
```

When you're happy with a plot, save it with `ggsave()`. It saves the last plot
you made, at a size you choose (in inches by default):

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggsave("atph-binding.png", width = 5, height = 4, dpi = 300)
ggsave("atph-binding.pdf", width = 5, height = 4)
```

## Saving results

To use the results in other software, such as Excel or Prism, save them as a
CSV file:

```{r}
#| eval: false
write.csv(fnorm, "fnorm.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(coefs, "binding-fits.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

## Using MO.Affinity Analysis's own results

If you have already done your analysis in MO.Affinity Analysis, you can read
its results directly instead of redoing them. A Compare Results (Chart) export
contains the mean response at each concentration and the fit:

```{r}
compare <- tidymst_example("dppr10-cy5_compare-fnorm.xlsx")

read_mst_dose_response(compare)

read_mst_fit(compare) |>
  select(target, model, kd, kd_confidence)
```

These data frames have the same columns as the ones above, so you can plot
them in the same way.
